title: Harvest & Beyond

learn.summary: Harvest is a skill of its own: picked at peak and kept picked, most crops produce more, taste better, and store longer. Beyond the harvest lie the multiplier skills — saving seed, stretching the season with simple protection, and keeping the growing habit alive indoors all winter. This is where a gardener becomes self-sustaining.

do: Harvest something — anything — from your garden or windowsill this week and cook with it the same day; note the flavor difference from store-bought

children.title: Timing & Storage

learn.summary: Pick leafy greens in the cool of morning when they are crisp, and keep harvesting beans, zucchini, and cucumbers small and often — an overlooked zucchini shuts the plant down. Storage splits by crop: tomatoes and basil never in the fridge; greens in the crisper in a bag with a paper towel; winter squash cured at 80-85°F for about 10 days then stored at 50-55°F; potatoes and onions cool, dark, and apart from each other.

do: Harvest your greens before 9am one day this week and compare their crispness to an afternoon-picked batch

children.title: Seed Saving

learn.summary: Save seed only from open-pollinated varieties — hybrids (F1) will not come true. Start with the easy selfers: tomatoes, beans, peas, and lettuce rarely cross and need no isolation. Dry seed thoroughly for 1-2 weeks, then store cool, dark, and dry in labeled envelopes; most stay viable 2-5 years, and each generation adapts slightly to your garden.

do: Save seed from one open-pollinated tomato or one dried bean pod this season, label the envelope with variety and date, and store it in a cool closet

children.title: Season Extension

learn.summary: A floating row cover adds 2-6°F of frost protection and can buy you weeks on both ends of the season for a few dollars; a cold frame or low tunnel effectively moves your garden about one zone south. Cold-hardy crops — spinach, kale, mache, carrots — survive hard freezes under cover and get sweeter. Fall timing is the catch: plants must be nearly full-size before day length collapses in November.

do: Buy one floating row cover and a few hoops this week, and use them to start greens 3-4 weeks earlier or keep them alive 3-4 weeks later than usual

children.title: Houseplants

learn.summary: Houseplants are horticulture in miniature and a year-round practice ground — the same light, water, and soil principles apply indoors. Overwatering is the number one killer: most houseplants want the top 1-2 inches of mix to dry out between waterings, and every pot needs a drainage hole. Start with near-unkillable pothos, snake plant, or ZZ plant, and match the plant to the window, not the decor.

do: Check every houseplant you own with the 2-inch finger test before its next watering, and move your most light-hungry plant to your brightest window
